E is correct!Incretins are released after eating and exaggerate insulin response (they extend the insulin response) Incretins include GLP-1 and Gastric inhibitory peptide (GIP) These are incretin mimetic drugs that try to act like these natural incretins. They extend the insulin response which means less insulin is needed after a meal. This is useful as when you take insulin it has a ceiling effect where it cannot get any lower than a certain point. Therefore if you have taken too much you will start to go hypo. With incretin mimetics this doesn't happen as they don't have a ceiling effect. Another advantage of these drugs is that they are not broken down by DPP4 (dipeptidyl-peptidase IV) which usually breaks down the incretins mentioned above. Therefore they last longer in the body. An example of one of these drugs is Saxagliptin. A problem with these drugs is that they increase the risk of pancreatic cancer and heart failure. They also cause headaches, nausea and vomiting.This was covered in Jeff's lecture on case 10. I took information from here and also the Oxford clinical handbook chapter on diabetes. Digoxin (a Na+/K+ ATPase blocker) will cause a transient increase in force of contraction by increasing levels of Ca2+ in the cytosol of the myocytes. This is because the Na+/K+ ATPase blockage causes the ions to move along the electrochemical gradient and flip the movement of ions through the NCX channel. This increases the intracellular calcium levels as more enters the cell than leaves it. The increased calcium stays high for longer so more forceful contractions occur. However, in the long term, digoxin can lead to a decline in force of contraction due to excessive calcium signalling resulting in calcium overload and activation of calmodulin-dependent phosphatases that dephosphorylate PKA and L-type calcium channels. This reduces the contractility of the heart.  From Case 6 Cardiac Failure lecture.
